section_summary: This section contains diplomatic despatches, State Department Far Eastern Affairs memoranda, and newspaper clippings from February to May 1936 concerning the aftermath of the Aizawa trial and the February 26 Incident in Japan. The documents trace the formation and policy agenda of the Hirota Cabinet, highlighting its moderate reform program, efforts to strengthen military discipline, and the purge or retirement of extremist army and naval officers. In addition, reporting addresses domestic economic measures—including interest rate cuts and bond conversions—as well as Japanese-Soviet border clashes in Manchukuo and Outer Mongolia, and broader international relations with the United States and Great Britain.

subfiles.about: Newspaper clippings reporting on courtroom testimony in the court-martial of Lieutenant-Colonel Saburo Aizawa and subsequent War Office personnel shifts to ease military tension.
subfiles.summary: Clippings continue Aizawa's court-martial defense citing national crisis and Kita's writings, plus War Minister Kawashima's measures easing tension via officer cautions and army reassignments.
subfiles.title: Press Clippings on the Aizawa Court-Martial and Army Personnel Adjustments

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum reviewing Tokyo Despatch No. 1758 regarding the reform policies and military dynamics of the Hirota Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Memo on Despatch 1758 summarizes Hirota Cabinet's moderate reforms—military discipline, thought education, agrarian relief—with no radical overhaul, noting growing disapproval of radical factions and an Ashida editorial.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Tokyo Embassy Despatch No. 1758 Regarding Policies of the Hirota Cabinet

subfiles.about: Despatch analyzing the domestic policies and reform program of the new Hirota Cabinet, transmitting an editorial from The Japan Times on the role of the military and reform.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports on the policy platform of the Hirota Cabinet based on speeches delivered by Premier Hirota and key ministers to prefectural governors on March 26, 1936. The despatch details proposed legislation affecting taxation, tariff revision, agrarian debt relief, and state control of key industries and the Tohoku Development Company. Grew emphasizes the government's aim to curb direct-action ultra-nationalism while making haste slowly on economic reforms, enclosing an editorial from The Japan Times analyzing internal ideological divisions within the military and the necessity of national defense preparations.
subfiles.title: Policies of the Hirota Cabinet

subfiles.about: Consular despatch transmitting a report on rumors and gendarme arrests in Harbin and Manchuria following the Tokyo February 26 Incident.
subfiles.summary: Lamont reports Kempeitai arrested over thirty Japanese, including a dozen officers, in Harbin amid Manchukuo-wide roundups reflecting sympathy with Tokyo insurgents among Manchuria's officers.
subfiles.title: The Tokyo Coup: Repercussions in Harbin

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum analyzing Tokyo Despatch No. 1784 on political, military, and economic developments following the February 26 Incident.
subfiles.summary: Memo on Despatch 1784 covers retained party politics, Peers vocational reform plans, abolishing the Cabinet Inquiry Council, and retiring 26 officers/6 generals as Terauchi's moderates secured army control.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Tokyo Embassy Despatch No. 1784 Regarding the Aftermath of the February 26th Incident

subfiles.about: Despatch reporting on political compromises, military purges, naval reorganization, and financial policies following the February 26 Incident, with an enclosed memorandum of conversation with Finance Minister Baba.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew provides an extensive review of the political, military, and economic consequences of the February 26 Incident. The despatch covers cabinet disputes over parliamentary counselors, reform proposals for the House of Peers advanced by Prince Konoye, and the sweeping disciplinary retirement of officers and admirals in both services. An enclosed memorandum by Commercial Attaché F. S. Williams recounts discussions with Finance Minister Eiichi Baba regarding interest rate cuts, bond conversion, taxation, and peaceful U.S.-Japanese relations, as well as an interview with newly appointed Ambassador to Belgium Saburo Kurusu.
subfiles.title: Aftermath of the February 26th Incident

subfiles.about: Despatch transmitting an article and an editorial from The Times of London examining the political influence of the Japanese military and frontier tensions with the Soviet Union.
subfiles.summary: Counselor of Embassy Ray Atherton transmits two press clippings from The Times of London analyzing the Japanese situation following the February 26 mutiny. The first enclosure, 'The Dualism of Japan,' explores how young military officers blended feudal samurai traditions, State Socialism, and Emperor-worship into a radical program for a Showa Restoration, contrasting their extremism with the moderate leadership of Hirota and Terauchi. The second enclosure, an editorial titled 'The Cloud in the Far East,' assesses dangerous border skirmishes between Manchukuo and Soviet-Outer Mongolian forces, warning of the risk that independent military actions might undermine civilian diplomacy.
subfiles.title: Press Comment on Japan
